lessons.title: Marginal Rate vs Effective Rate: The Most Misunderstood Idea in Indian Tax

body.text: Your marginal rate tells you what the next rupee costs. Your effective rate tells you what all your rupees cost on average. Use the marginal rate for every decision and the effective rate only for budgeting.

children.text: When someone says "I'm in the 30% bracket", they are quoting one number. But every taxpayer actually has two tax rates, and they answer completely different questions. Mixing them up leads to turning down raises, overpaying for tax-saving products and misjudging what an FD really earns you.

markDefs.definition: The rate of tax on the next rupee of income. For most taxpayers it is the rate of their top slab, increased by the 4% cess.
Total tax paid divided by income. Also called the average tax rate. Always lower than the marginal rate in a progressive system.

points: How much of my raise or bonus will I keep?

points: What share of my income goes to income tax overall?
How much should I set aside for tax each month?
How does my tax burden compare with last year's?
How does my tax burden compare with a friend's?
Never the right number for a yes or no financial decision

body.title: The Effective Rate Chases the Marginal Rate but Never Catches It

children.text: The effective rate is always well below the marginal rate because the lower slabs keep dragging the average down. Even at ₹50 lakh, where the marginal rate has been 30% for ₹26 lakh of income, the effective slab rate is only 21.6%. As income grows it creeps closer to 30%, but the ₹3,00,000 saved in the lower slabs means it can never reach it on the slab table alone.

body.label: Your Real Marginal Rate Includes Cess
body.context: The 4% health and education cess applies to every rupee of tax. So the 30% slab is really 31.2%, 25% is 26%, 20% is 20.8% and 15% is 15.6%. Surcharge, covered in Chapter 3, raises it further for high earners.

body.text: The marginal rate is not always a slab rate. Just above ₹12 lakh under the new regime, marginal relief means almost every extra rupee goes to tax for a short stretch, a marginal rate close to 100%. Just above ₹5 lakh under the old regime, losing the rebate has a similar effect. And for incomes that cross surcharge thresholds, the marginal rate can briefly spike too. Chapter 3 shows exactly where these zones are.

children.text: Which Income Do You Divide By?

Effective rate figures quoted online are often not comparable, because people divide by different numbers. Take Priya from Chapter 1. Her gross salary is ₹18,75,000, her Total Income after the standard deduction is ₹18,00,000, and her tax including 4% cess is ₹1,66,400.

Neither 9.24% nor 8.87% is wrong; they answer slightly different questions. What matters is using the same base when comparing years or people. For budgeting take-home pay, dividing by gross salary is usually the more useful figure.
Using the Marginal Rate to Make Real Decisions

Decision 1: side income. Nikhil, an architect in Ahmedabad on the new regime, has Total Income of ₹22,00,000. A developer offers him ₹1,00,000 for a weekend design project. His marginal rate is 25% plus cess, or 26%. The project adds ₹26,000 of tax, and he keeps ₹74,000. His effective rate of 11.4% would have wrongly suggested he keeps about ₹88,600.

Decision 2: what an FD really earns. FD interest is added to your income and taxed at your marginal rate. A 7% FD from SBI earns a very different return for a taxpayer in the 15% slab than for one in the 30% slab.

body.caption: Post-Tax Return on a 7% FD by Marginal Rate

body.text: Decision 3, the value of a deduction, works the same way in reverse. A deduction removes income from your top slab, so it saves tax at your marginal rate. You saw this in Chapter 1: Sneha's ₹70,000 employer NPS deduction saved ₹10,920 at a marginal rate of 15.6%, not ₹70,000 and not her effective rate.

body.title: Effective Slab Rate at ₹26 Lakh
body.prompt: Farah, a senior manager at a Hyderabad pharma company, has Total Income of ₹26,00,000 under the new regime. What is her effective rate on slab tax, before cess, as a percentage? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Slab tax is ₹3,00,000 + 30% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,60,000. Divided by ₹26,00,000, that is 13.85%. Her marginal rate is 30% on slab tax, or 31.2% with cess, more than double her effective rate.

body.title: Pick the Right Rate
body.question: Vivek has Total Income of ₹18,00,000 under the new regime. His effective rate including cess is about 9.2%. He is deciding whether to pay ₹50,000 into a product that gives him a ₹50,000 deduction. Which figure best estimates his tax saving?
body.explanation: The ₹50,000 comes out of his 20% slab (16 to 20 lakh), so the saving is 20% × ₹50,000 = ₹10,000 plus ₹400 cess. Using the effective rate understates the saving by more than half. Note also that only a few deductions, such as employer NPS contributions, are allowed under the new regime at all.

body.title: Name the Rate
body.textWithBlank: To work out how much of a ₹2 lakh bonus you will keep after tax, you should use your ___ rate.
body.explanation: The bonus sits on top of your existing income, so it is taxed at the rate of the slabs it falls into, not at your average rate. If the bonus is large enough to push you into the next slab, part of it is taxed at the higher rate.

body.title: PPF or FD?
body.scenario: Divya, a chartered accountant in Kolkata on the new regime, has Total Income of ₹19,00,000. She wants to invest ₹1,50,000 for the long term and is comparing a bank FD at 7.5%, fully taxable, with PPF at 7.1%, fully tax-free. Assume both rates hold for the whole period. Her friend says: "FD pays more, obviously."
body.prompt: Which option gives Divya the better return after tax, and by how much per year on ₹1,50,000?
body.modelAnswer: Divya's marginal rate is 20% plus cess, or 20.8%. The FD's post-tax return is 7.5% × (1 − 0.208) = 5.94%, or ₹8,910 a year on ₹1,50,000. PPF's 7.1% is tax-free, or ₹10,650 a year. PPF wins by 1.16 percentage points, about ₹1,740 a year before compounding. The friend compared pre-tax rates. The comparison only works after adjusting for the marginal rate, and the trade-off is PPF's 15-year lock-in versus the FD's flexibility. Note that under the new regime Divya gets no deduction for the PPF deposit itself; the advantage here comes purely from tax-free interest.

points: Marginal rate is the tax on the next rupee; effective rate is total tax divided by income
In a progressive system the effective rate is always below the marginal rate, and on the new regime slab table it never reaches 30%
Add 4% cess to get your true marginal rate: 30% becomes 31.2%, 20% becomes 20.8%
Use the marginal rate for raises, side income, deductions, FD returns and tax-free vs taxable comparisons
Use the effective rate only for budgeting and comparisons, and always state which income you divided by
Near the rebate limit and surcharge thresholds, the marginal rate can briefly be far higher than your slab rate

body.text: Rates shown are for the new regime for tax year 2026-27. FD and PPF rates are illustrative and change over time. This lesson is for education only and is not tax or investment advice.
